problem: VLM-guided frontier exploration in EQA (e.g. 3D-Mem) lets an overconfident, miscalibrated VLM pick the single next frontier at each step, causing back-and-forth frontier oscillations, inefficient paths, timeouts and worse answers. Prior calibration work only calibrates episode-level behavior such as when to stop.
motivation: Exploration efficiency directly drives the quality and speed of EQA answers, and long prompts and VLM overconfidence make step-level VLM decisions brittle. The observation is that a VLM is more reliable at flagging clearly bad frontiers than at picking the best one, so its role can be reduced to conservative pruning.
key_idea: Use the VLM only to prune likely-bad frontiers via human-calibrated ECDF p-values and a Holm-Bonferroni-style step-down rule, then pick the closest surviving frontier with a coverage-based planner.
insight: Separating semantic pruning from planning turns VLM overconfidence into stable behavior: when the VLM is confident, one frontier survives; when it is uncertain, many survive and the planner decides. The ablation on exploration strategy shows pruning plus closest-frontier (overall 39.54) beats both VLM-only (37.82) and closest-only (36.93) on EXPRESS-Bench. The label-noise ablation shows the calibration is robust: 5% flipped labels leave EAC at 34.3, and 10% drops it to 32.3, still above 3D-Mem's 29.2.
method: VLM frontier confidence: tag each frontier snapshot with a letter token in the 3D-Mem prompt, take next-token logits, and softmax them into per-frontier confidences c_t^i.
Step-wise normalized score: s_t^i = c_t^i / max_j c_t^j, which makes scores comparable across steps and episodes.

Human-labeled calibration: two annotators labeled about 5,500 frontiers (about 3,600 bad) from the 348 held-out A-EQA questions; per-step argmax frontiers are excluded and an ECDF of bad-frontier scores is fitted.
p-value mapping: p = (1 + N(1 - F_bad(s))) / (1 + N), a right-tail p-value; a high p means the score is typical of a bad frontier.

Holm-Bonferroni step-down pruning: sort p-values ascending and keep frontiers while p_(j) <= alpha/(K-j+1); alpha is a behavioral pruning-strictness knob (0.5 used, tuned on 252 EXPRESS-Bench questions).
Coverage planner: choose the surviving frontier with minimum geodesic distance from the agent, ignoring the VLM's preference, and re-run at every step inside 3D-Mem.
Metrics: path curvature (mean turning angle) as an oscillation proxy and coverage AUC.

setting.backbone: Qwen2.5-VL-32B (frozen, agent); Qwen3-VL-30B for grounded scoring
setting.training_data: none (training-free); an ECDF is fitted on about 5,500 human-labeled frontiers from 348 held-out OpenEQA A-EQA questions

results: On OpenEQA, Prune-Then-Plan reaches SPL 29.1 and LLM-Match 34.3, versus 3D-Mem 24.7/29.2 and Fine-EQA 19.5/25.7. On EXPRESS-Bench it gives 25.7/39.5 versus 3D-Mem 25.6/37.8, with 31-46% lower curvature and about 50% higher coverage by step 50. The abstract claims up to 49% SPL and 33% LLM-Match relative gains, over Fine-EQA.
limitations: Gains over 3D-Mem on EXPRESS-Bench are marginal (SPL 25.7 vs 25.6), since short-horizon questions dominate.
Requires human-labeled calibration data and a single ECDF shared across question types; location questions are sensitive to alpha (peak near 0.6), suggesting category-specific ECDFs are needed.
Alpha is a heuristic hyperparameter with no formal error guarantee; only Qwen2.5-VL-32B was tested and one 3D-Mem base pipeline was used.
